France and the UAE proposed renewing sanctions and continuing expert monitoring in S/2023/638 to support Mali’s peace agreement and an orderly drawdown. France voted yes. Russia’s sole negative vote vetoed the draft, which received 13–1–1. Russia said the existing approach neglected the transitional Government’s concerns. Its separate draft S/2023/639 proposed a final extension and immediate dissolution of the Panel of Experts. Russia voted yes and France abstained. It failed 1–1–13 for insufficient affirmative votes. Both drafts proposed temporary extensions. They differed over whether the Panel should continue and whether the extension should be final. Neither draft was adopted and neither vote created new authority.

The Council adopted the United Kingdom’s draft S/2022/980 as resolution 2669 (2022), 12–0–3. China, India and Russia abstained. India held the Council presidency. The President called the vote and announced adoption. In its national capacity India explained its abstention, citing neighbours’ concerns and favouring quiet, constructive diplomacy. The UK voted yes after consultations and stressed ending violence, humanitarian access and ASEAN’s efforts. Both acknowledged regional consultation, while their votes differed. The resolution demands an immediate end to violence, calls for humanitarian access and recognises ASEAN’s central role. It requests an oral report to the Council by 15 March 2023 from the Secretary-General or his Special Envoy, coordinated with the ASEAN Special Envoy, on UN support for the Five-Point Consensus.

On 27 June 2018 the Council adopted Peru’s draft S/2018/628 as Resolution 2422, 14–0–1 with Russia abstaining. Under Chapter VII it appointed Serge Brammertz Mechanism Prosecutor from 1 July 2018 until 30 June 2020, concluded its progress review and underlined full state cooperation. Peru called for Council unity and said combating impunity required states to enforce sentences, execute warrants and answer assistance requests. Russia linked its abstention to earlier staffing concerns and criticized administration. It questioned Mladić’s care and recalled requesting temporary release to Russia for treatment under Russian guarantees if prison doctors could not provide it. Serbia, participating without a vote, objected that the Mechanism refused temporary medical release despite Serbian guarantees. Serbia said it met its cooperation obligations and would prosecute war crimes regardless of nationality.
